Paper Title: Modeling costs of turns in route planning
Research Problem: GIS road representations assign costs to edges/nodes, failing to model intersection turn delays and angle costs, leading to erratic zig-zag paths
Methodology: Mathematical transformation of directed graph to line graph (pseudo-dual) where vertices represent edges and edges represent turns; applies standard Dijkstra/A*
Relevant Findings: Modest turn penalties (10m-30m equivalent) eliminate zig-zags; line graph scales to ~3x vertices and ~4.5x edges in planar grids
Limitations: Line graph materialization increases storage by 3-5x; assumes static geometric angles without dynamic traffic queues or vehicle-specific physics
Relevance to Our Work: Foundational theory for our state-expanded A* search tracking (prev_node, curr_node) without explicit line graph construction

Paper Title: Efficient Routing in Road Networks with Turn Costs
Publication Venue: Proc. 10th Int. Symp. on Experimental Algorithms (SEA 2011), LNCS 6630, 100-111
Research Problem: Hierarchical speedup techniques (Contraction Hierarchies) ignore turn costs; line graph expansion causes 5-10x memory explosion and destroys preprocessing efficiency
Methodology: Edge-Based Contraction Hierarchies (EBCH) contracting edges; junction turn tables; bidirectional edge-state query search on continental networks
Relevant Findings: Query times under 1.5 ms with 2.5-3.5x preprocessing overhead and 2x memory increase compared to node-based CH
Limitations: Static turn costs precomputed into shortcuts; cannot dynamically adjust turn penalties or multi-criteria weights at query time; car-centric turn assumptions
Relevance to Our Work: Contrasts our runtime-customizable A* against static hierarchy preprocessing; proves need for edge-state search without full line graph

Paper Title: Customizable Route Planning in Road Networks
Authors: Daniel Delling, Andrew V. Goldberg, Thomas Pajor, Renato F. Werneck
Research Problem: Hierarchical routing algorithms bake metrics into shortcuts, requiring complete re-preprocessing when vehicle profiles, traffic, or preferences change
Methodology: Three-phase architecture (CRP): metric-independent graph partitioning (PUNCH), sub-second metric customization across overlay cells, multi-level query search
Relevant Findings: Customizes new vehicle metrics in under 1 second; point-to-point queries in under 2.5 ms on continent-scale networks (~50M edges)
Limitations: Complex graph partitioning infrastructure required; optimized for web-scale continental routing; less suited for lightweight embedded/local deployment
Relevance to Our Work: Justifies decoupling metric definitions from topology; validates our custom multi-attribute edge impedance parameters

Authors: Hannah Bast, Daniel Delling, Andrew V. Goldberg, Matthias Müller-Hannemann, Thomas Pajor, Peter Sanders, Dorothea Wagner, Renato F. Werneck
Publication Venue: Algorithm Engineering: Selected Results and Surveys, LNCS 9220, 19-80
Research Problem: Comprehensive survey of shortest-path speed-up techniques, multi-criteria optimization, and turn-cost handling in continental and transit networks
Methodology: Exhaustive survey and algorithmic taxonomy analyzing Dijkstra, A*, ALT, Contraction Hierarchies, CRP, and Pareto bicriteria search
Relevant Findings: Proves exact Pareto multi-criteria routing is NP-hard with exponential path growth; linear scalarization is necessary for interactive queries
Limitations: Surveys car and transit networks exclusively; zero coverage of motorized two-wheeler kinematics or developing-city mixed traffic
Relevance to Our Work: Definitive algorithmic reference; justifies our linear scalarized impedance model and dynamic state tracking over NP-hard Pareto enumeration

Paper Title: Entropy-Based k Shortest-Path Routing for Motorcycles: A Simulated Case Study in Jakarta
Authors: Muhamad Asvial, M. Faridz Gita Pandoyo, Ajib Setyo Arifin
Publication Venue: Int. J. Advanced Computer Science and Applications (IJACSA), 11(7), 438-445
Research Problem: Commercial navigation systems direct all motorcycles onto major arterials, exacerbating traffic bottlenecks and ignoring narrow road capability
Methodology: OpenStreetMap road network ingestion; modified pgRouting kSP algorithm with entropy balancing based on simulated vehicle traffic footprint
Relevant Findings: Motorcycle routing through narrow residential streets achieves up to 8% travel time reduction on trips <10 km vs Google Maps
Limitations: Completely ignores turn penalties (turn cost = 0); tested on only 6 simulated OD pairs; manual synthetic traffic footprint; no heuristic admissibility proof
Relevance to Our Work: Primary direct competitor on OSM motorcycle routing; demonstrates the critical gap our turn-aware state-expanded A* directly solves

Paper Title: Lane-Filtering Behavior of Motorcycle Riders at Signalized Urban Intersections
Authors: Thanapol Promraksa, Thaned Satiennam, Wichuda Satiennam, Nopadon Kronprasert
Research Problem: Lack of empirical quantification of motorcycle lane-filtering lateral clearance, speeds, and queue discharge kinematics at signalized urban junctions
Methodology: Video analysis across 4 signalized intersections in Thailand; statistical modeling of lateral gap thresholds and filtering speed distributions
Relevant Findings: Motorcycles filter through lateral clearances of 0.75m-0.90m between stopped cars at 12-25 km/h, significantly bypassing intersection queue delay
Limitations: Microscopic empirical study confined to 4 physical intersections; does not provide a macroscopic network routing algorithm
Relevance to Our Work: Provides empirical physical grounding for two-wheeler filtering capability and why car-centric road hierarchies fail in Asian cities

Paper Title: Modeling lateral placement and movement of vehicles on urban undivided roads in mixed traffic: A case study of India
Authors: P. B. Kotagi, P. Raj, G. Asaithambi
Publication Venue: J. Traffic and Transportation Engineering (English Edition), 7(6), 860-873
Research Problem: Vehicular lateral movement and non-lane discipline in heterogeneous Indian traffic are poorly modeled by conventional lane-based traffic theory
Methodology: Videographic trajectory extraction and statistical modeling on undivided urban arterials in Bengaluru and Mangaluru, India
Relevant Findings: Two-wheelers occupy small lateral clearances (0.3m-0.6m) and exploit gaps dynamically, maintaining forward progression when cars are stalled
Limitations: Microscopic segment-level analysis; does not translate lateral kinematic advantage into network-level routing cost functions
Relevance to Our Work: Empirically validates mixed traffic behavior in Bengaluru; justifies discounting two-wheeler impedance on non-arterial road fabrics

Paper Title: Modeling Maneuverability of Motorized Two-Wheelers during Filtering in Urban Roads
Research Problem: Lack of microscopic kinematic models capturing motorized two-wheeler filtering maneuvers between slow-moving or stationary vehicular queues in India
Methodology: Cellular automata model calibrated with empirical trajectory data on urban corridors in Mumbai, India
Relevant Findings: Two-wheelers achieve 35%-48% higher average velocities than passenger cars under congested mixed traffic via continuous filtering
Limitations: Single-corridor cellular automata simulation; lacks graph-theoretic path planning or intersection turn delay modeling
Relevance to Our Work: Quantifies the speed differential between two-wheelers and cars in congested Indian traffic, supporting peak-hour hierarchy inversion

Paper Title: Identifying the role of route choice behavior of motorcycle riders in microscopic simulation modeling under mixed traffic conditions
Authors: Siti Raudhatul Fadilah, Hiroaki Nishiuchi, Anh Minh Ngoc
Research Problem: Standard route choice models assume travelers optimize travel time or distance, ignoring vehicle-specific route selection behavior of motorcyclists
Methodology: Revealed and stated preference surveys; multinomial logit and mixed logit route-choice modeling in mixed traffic (Indonesia)
Relevant Findings: Motorcycle commuters exhibit strong preference for secondary/residential roads and actively accept distance detours to avoid queuing and safety risks
Limitations: Econometric behavioral study; does not implement an algorithmic graph routing engine or A* optimization framework
Relevance to Our Work: Directly supports our inverted road hierarchy hypothesis: two-wheeler riders systematically avoid primary arterial vehicle queues

Paper Title: OSMnx: New methods for acquiring, constructing, analyzing, and visualizing complex street networks
Research Problem: Acquiring, correcting, and analyzing real-world complex street networks from OpenStreetMap is historically fragmented, error-prone, and inconsistent
Methodology: Python library formulation automating OSM downloading, topological correction (simplification, node consolidation), and NetworkX export
Relevant Findings: Enables programmatic topological extraction of non-planar directed multi-graphs with complete edge attributes (highway, length, bridge, surface)
Limitations: Static graph model; does not implement dynamic state-expanded search algorithms or vehicle-specific impedance weighting out of the box
Relevance to Our Work: Foundational infrastructure paper for our Bengaluru street network extraction and attribute management in GraphManager

Publication Venue: Proc. 19th ACM SIGSPATIAL Int. Conf. on Advances in GIS (GIS '11), 513-516
Research Problem: Real-time routing on OpenStreetMap graphs on commodity hardware with sub-second queries across continent-sized networks
Methodology: Open Source Routing Machine (OSRM) engineering Contraction Hierarchies directly on OpenStreetMap topological data
Relevant Findings: Sub-millisecond car queries on European OSM graph; introduces Lua-based speed and road classification profiles
Limitations: Enforces strict automobile-centric speed hierarchy where primary arterials are prioritized; CH shortcuts prevent runtime turn customization
Relevance to Our Work: Represents the standard automobile routing baseline that our two-wheeler engine explicitly challenges during urban peak saturation

Paper Title: Real-Time Bengaluru City Traffic Congestion Prediction Using Deep Learning Models
Authors: Karigowda Dhananjaya Kumar, Mandya Lingaiah Anitha, Manchanahali Narsegowda Veena
Publication Venue: Int. J. Transport Development and Integration, 9(3), 619-628
Research Problem: Accurate forecasting of peak-hour traffic volume and saturation points across major arterial corridors in Bengaluru, India
Methodology: Benchmarks 1D CNN, LSTM, and SVR deep learning architectures on historical volume and weather sensor datasets from central Bengaluru
Relevant Findings: Identifies 100% volume saturation on Hosur Road, MG Road / Trinity Circle, and Yeshwanthpur; achieves MAE = 6.02 with 1D CNN
Limitations: Unclosed loop: terminates at prediction; does not provide a routing engine or alternative path generation mechanism for congested corridors
Relevance to Our Work: Serves as our empirical ground-truth baseline for saturated corridors in central Bengaluru, justifying our arterial impedance penalties

Paper Title: A Formal Basis for the Heuristic Determination of Minimum Cost Paths
Authors: Peter E. Hart, Nils J. Nilsson, Bertram Raphael
Publication Venue: IEEE Transactions on Systems Science and Cybernetics, SSC-4(2), 100-107
Research Problem: Mathematical formulation and optimality proof for heuristic search algorithms operating on graphs
Methodology: Formal mathematical derivation of A* algorithm, admissibility (h(n) <= h*(n)), and consistency (monotonicity triangle inequality)
Relevant Findings: Proves A* is guaranteed to find optimal minimum-cost path if heuristic never overestimates true remaining cost; consistency avoids re-openings
Limitations: Theoretical paper; assumes scalar node-based graph traversal costs without edge-dependent turn deflection costs
Relevance to Our Work: Foundational mathematical authority for our proof that scaling Haversine distance by 0.8 preserves strict admissibility and consistency under turn penalties

Paper Title: Computing the Shortest Path: A* Search Meets Graph Theory
Publication Venue: Proc. 16th ACM-SIAM Symp. on Discrete Algorithms (SODA 2005), 156-165
Research Problem: Euclidean heuristics for A* on road networks are weak because road distances exceed straight-line Euclidean distance by 20%-40%
Methodology: ALT algorithm: Precomputes distances to a small set of landmark nodes, using triangle inequality to generate tight admissible lower bounds
Relevant Findings: Achieves significant speedups over standard A* on continental networks without contracting or mutating the graph topology
Limitations: Landmark precomputation consumes memory; landmark heuristics assume static costs; changing edge multipliers requires landmark recomputation
Relevance to Our Work: Provides theoretical context on heuristic lower-bounding in road networks, contrasting landmark precomputation with our zero-preprocessing Haversine bound

Paper Title: A heuristic algorithm for solving hazardous materials distribution problems
Authors: Konstantinos G. Zografos, Konstantinos N. Androutsopoulos
Research Problem: Hazardous material transport requires avoiding sharp, dangerous turns and congested intersections while balancing travel risk and distance
Methodology: Bicriteria shortest-path formulation on edge-expanded road network; heuristic branch-and-bound evaluating physical turn angles and delays
Relevant Findings: Demonstrates that incorporating turn penalties significantly reduces hazardous maneuver exposure with modest detour trade-offs
Limitations: Focuses on heavy hazardous freight vehicles; highly specialized risk metrics; computationally heavy branch-and-bound search
Relevance to Our Work: Demonstrates that multi-objective trade-offs between physical distance and turn maneuvers are vital in specialized vehicle routing

Paper Title: The minimum route problem for networks with turn penalties and prohibitions
Authors: R. F. Kirby, R. B. Potts
Research Problem: Shortest path algorithms assume link costs are independent, failing when intersection turns incur delays or prohibitions
Methodology: Original network expansion transforming links and permissible turns into expanded state representation for shortest-path optimization
Relevant Findings: Proved that expanding nodes into turn states allows standard shortest-path algorithms to handle arbitrary non-negative turn penalties
Limitations: Focuses on basic traffic assignment; theoretical graph transformation without vehicle-differentiated cost models or spatial heuristics
Relevance to Our Work: Landmark origin paper for turn-expanded graph representations, establishing theoretical precedent for state-expanded search

Authors: Ittai Abraham, Daniel Delling, Andrew V. Goldberg, Renato F. Werneck
Research Problem: Generating human-meaningful alternative routes on road networks; classic Yen's kSP fails due to sharing >90% edges with single-block detours
Methodology: Formal definition of alternative route quality: bounded detour (<= 1.20), limited sharing (<= 0.70), and local optimality; proposes Via-Node and Penalty methods
Relevant Findings: Evaluates via-node heuristics on continental highway networks, discovering meaningful alternative trunk corridors
Limitations: Highway via-node plateaus fail in dense planar urban grids lacking grade-separated expressways; tested only on car highway networks
Relevance to Our Work: Formal quality criteria (detour <= 20%, overlap <= 70%) provide the mathematical benchmarks for evaluating alternative path candidates
